segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now faith is the reality of things hoped for, the proof of things not seen.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For by it the ancients were attested.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: By faith we understand that the worlds were set in order by God’s word, so that what is seen did not come into being from things that appear.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: By faith Abel offered to God a greater sacrifice than Cain, through which he was attested as righteous, God attesting to his gifts; and through it, though he died, he still speaks.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: By faith Enoch was taken away so that he did not see death, and he was not found, because God had taken him away. For it is attested that before he was taken away he had pleased God,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and without faith it is impossible to please him, for whoever approaches God must believe that he exists and that he rewards those who seek him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: By faith Noah, warned by God about things not yet seen, in reverent fear built an ark to save his household. Through this he condemned the world and became an heir of the righteousness that accords with faith.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: By faith Abraham, when he was called, obeyed and went out to a place he was going to receive as an inheritance; and he went out not knowing where he was going.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: By faith he lived as a foreigner in the land of the promise, as in a land belonging to another, dwelling in tents with Isaac and Jacob, fellow heirs of the same promise;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for he was waiting for the city that has foundations, whose designer and builder is God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: By faith, together with Sarah herself, he received power to father offspring, even past the age for it, since he considered the one who had promised faithful.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And so from one man, and him as good as dead, were born descendants as many as the stars of the sky in number and as countless as the sand along the shore of the sea.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: All these died in faith, without having received the promises, but having seen them from afar and greeted them, and having confessed that they were strangers and temporary residents on the earth.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For people who say such things make it clear that they are seeking a homeland.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And if they had been thinking of the one they had left, they would have had opportunity to return.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But as it is, they long for a better one, that is, a heavenly one. Therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God, for he has prepared a city for them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: By faith Abraham, when he was tested, offered up Isaac. The one who had accepted the promises was offering his one and only son,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: he to whom it had been said,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “It is through Isaac that your offspring will be named.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He reasoned that God is able to raise even from the dead, from which, figuratively speaking, he did receive him back.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: By faith Isaac blessed Jacob and Esau, even regarding things to come.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: By faith Jacob, as he was dying, blessed each of Joseph’s sons, and bowed in worship over the top of his staff.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: By faith Joseph, at the end of his life, spoke of the exodus of the sons of Israel and gave instructions about his bones.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: By faith Moses, when he was born, was hidden for three months by his parents, because they saw that the child was beautiful, and they were not afraid of the king’s edict.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: By faith Moses, when he had grown up, refused to be called a son of Pharaoh’s daughter,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: choosing rather to be mistreated along with the people of God than to have the short-lived enjoyment of sin,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: considering the reproach of Christ greater wealth than the treasures of Egypt, for he was looking ahead to the reward.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: By faith he left Egypt, not fearing the king’s anger, for he persevered as one who sees the unseen one.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: By faith he kept the Passover and the sprinkling of the blood, so that the destroyer of the firstborn would not touch them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: By faith they crossed the Red Sea as if over dry land; when the Egyptians tried it, they were swallowed up.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: By faith the walls of Jericho fell after being encircled for seven days.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: By faith Rahab the prostitute did not perish with those who disobeyed, because she had welcomed the spies in peace.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And what more should I say? For time will fail me if I tell of Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, of David and Samuel and the prophets,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: who through faith conquered kingdoms, administered justice, obtained promises, shut the mouths of lions,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: quenched the power of fire, escaped the edge of the sword, were made powerful out of weakness, became mighty in war, routed the armies of foreigners.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Women received their dead back by resurrection. Others were tortured, refusing to accept release, so that they might obtain a better resurrection.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Still others experienced mockery and floggings, and even chains and imprisonment.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They were stoned, they were sawn in two, they were put to death by the sword. They went about in sheepskins and goatskins, destitute, afflicted, mistreated,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: people of whom the world was not worthy, wandering over deserts and mountains and in caves and holes in the ground.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And all these, though attested through their faith, did not receive the promise,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: because God had provided something better with us in view, so that apart from us they would not be brought to completion.

notes.note: Most modern versions render this word as an inner state, 'assurance' or 'confidence', paired with 'conviction' for the second term. In the usage of the period the word normally refers to something objective: the underlying reality of a thing, or in legal documents a guarantee of ownership. Its partner term likewise means 'proof' or 'evidence', not a feeling of being convinced. The subjective reading remains common, and the sense here is disputed.

notes.traditional: were commended; obtained a good report
notes.note: The verb means 'to bear witness', and in the passive 'to have witness borne to one', usually favourably. 'Commended' gives the favourable sense but hides the language of testimony, which recurs in verses 4, 5 and 39 and leads to the 'cloud of witnesses' at the start of the next chapter. The implied witness is God, speaking through Scripture.

The Greek word is literally 'the ages'. In Jewish Greek the plural could mean the created world in its whole extent of time and space, and the reference to 'what is seen' favours that sense here. Some interpreters keep 'the ages' and take the verse to mean God's ordering of history.

notes.traditional: By faith Sarah herself received power to conceive
notes.note: The earliest manuscripts had no accents or iota subscripts, so the words 'Sarah herself' can be read as the subject or as a dative, 'together with Sarah herself'. SBLGNT prints the dative, which makes Abraham the subject. This suits the Greek phrase used, which is the ordinary expression for the father's part in conception, and it suits verse 12, where 'one man' is Abraham. Many translations take Sarah as the subject, and some manuscripts add that she was barren.

The word means 'only one of its kind' and was used of an only child; its second element is related to 'kind', not to 'beget'. Isaac was not Abraham's only son, since Ishmael was born first, but he was the unique son through whom the promise ran. 'One and only' is the usual modern rendering, though a minority of scholars have recently defended 'only begotten'.

The Greek is literally 'in a parable'. It may mean that Isaac's rescue was as good as a return from the dead, or that the event served as a symbol pointing forward, either to resurrection in general or to Christ's. The translation leaves both possibilities open.

notes.phrase: over the top of his staff
notes.traditional: leaning upon the top of his staff
notes.note: This follows the Greek translation of Genesis 47:31. The Hebrew text as traditionally vocalised says that Jacob bowed at the head of his bed; the same Hebrew consonants can be read as either 'bed' or 'staff'. The author of Hebrews regularly quotes Scripture in its Greek form.

The phrase can mean abuse like that which Christ bore, abuse suffered for Christ's sake, or the abuse that falls on God's anointed, here his people. It echoes the language of Psalm 89:50–51, where God's 'anointed' is taunted. The author most likely sees Moses as sharing in advance the disgrace Christ would bear, a theme taken up again at 13:13.

Greek has a single word-family where English has two: righteous and just, righteousness and justice. This translation normally uses 'righteous' and 'righteousness', as in verses 4 and 7. Here the list concerns the deeds of judges, kings and prophets, so fair ruling is probably meant, and many modern versions also have 'justice'. 'Did what was right' is also possible.

The verb refers to a specific instrument of torture on which victims were stretched and beaten to death. The allusion is almost certainly to the martyrs of 2 Maccabees 6–7, the aged scribe Eleazar and seven brothers, who refused to save themselves by breaking the law and declared their hope of resurrection. The 'better resurrection' is contrasted with the return to ordinary life in the first half of the verse.

notes.traditional: they were sawn asunder, were tempted
notes.note: Many manuscripts add 'they were tempted' or 'they were tested' before or after these words, and the King James Version includes it. SBLGNT omits it as a probable scribal addition or duplication of the similar-looking Greek word for 'sawn in two'. Being sawn in two recalls a Jewish tradition about the death of the prophet Isaiah.

The verb means to bring something to its goal or finished state. 'Made perfect' is the traditional rendering throughout Hebrews, but in modern English it suggests flawlessness, whereas the point is that the faithful of earlier times reach the promised goal only together with those who come after. Most translations keep 'made perfect'.

candidates.reason: Occurs in Hebrews 1:3, 3:14, 11:1 and 2 Corinthians 9:4, 11:17, and translators split between objective senses (reality, substance, guarantee) and subjective ones (assurance, confidence), which changes the definition of faith.

The passive is rendered variously as 'commended', 'approved', 'well spoken of' or 'attested' across Acts, the Pastorals and Hebrews, and the link to μάρτυς ('witness', 12:1) is lost if the English varies.
A thematic word in Hebrews, also found in John, Luke, Philippians and 1 John, where 'make perfect' and 'complete' compete, and the reader needs one rendering to follow the argument.
The plural in Hebrews 1:2 and 11:3 is rendered 'worlds', 'universe' or 'ages', and needs to be coordinated with the temporal uses ('age', 'forever') elsewhere.
Very frequent across the Gospels, Acts and Revelation, where 'worship', 'bow down' and 'pay homage' carry different implications about the object of the act.
